messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Stock Broker
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Idealized Families: Happy families, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 38, Linh Nguyen had built a life that looked fast, competent, and tightly managed from the outside. She worked as a stock broker in a noisy Manhattan office where phones rang across the floor, traders shouted bids, and market alerts burst from speakers without warning. She lived with her partner in a high-rise downtown and had once taken some pride in how well she could tolerate pressure. What brought her to treatment was not a single new incident but the recognition, after many months, that her world had been shrinking around a past she still could not make feel finished.

The stalking had begun after a brief relationship ended. At first it came as repeated messages, then long voicemails left late at night, then appearances that felt impossible to explain away. He seemed to know where she had been, what train she had taken, when she had gone to dinner. More than once she caught the smell of alcohol before she saw him and felt her body go cold, because that odor had become part of how he arrived into her life: outside her building entrance, too close behind her on the sidewalk, once waiting near her car and speaking in a slurred, insistent voice as if he still had a claim on her. The worst moments were not dramatic in a cinematic sense; that was part of what made them so destabilizing. They were made of repetition, intrusion, and the steady collapse of any expectation that she could predict where she would be safe. By the end she was jumping at every sound in the hallway, bracing whenever a sudden crash came from the street below, already scanning for whether he had found her again.

What she has struggled to explain in the months since is that the memory does not sit in the past in an ordinary way. When she talks about those weeks, Linh often pauses and says it sounds exaggerated even to her, “like something that happened to somebody else,” because the extremity of living under constant watch still feels unreal. Yet when it comes back, it does not return as a distant narrative. She feels as though she is back inside it immediately, with the same surge of terror she had when she realized he could appear anywhere. That quality of reliving has made seemingly ordinary moments in the present feel charged with danger. On the trading floor, a burst of shouting or a slammed door can pull her straight into that older fear before she has even oriented herself. Passing someone on the street with alcohol on his breath can make her chest tighten and her mind race to where she can exit. Seeing a cheerful family in a restaurant window or in the lobby of her building can unsettle her in a way she finds hard to justify, because it throws her against a painful sense of distance from normal life; the contrast makes the stalking feel both bizarre and vividly present, as if everyone else belongs to a safer world she somehow lost access to.

Because the memory arrives with such immediacy, Linh has become increasingly preoccupied with avoiding moments that might set it off. At work she keeps one earbud in even when she is not listening to anything, partly to blunt the shock of sudden loud sounds on the floor. She has started taking side streets home to avoid the bars near her apartment, not wanting to catch the smell of liquor drifting out onto the sidewalk. Her partner has noticed that she becomes quiet and withdrawn when they pass families at brunch spots on weekends, her expression flattening as if she has gone somewhere else. Linh knows these reactions look disproportionate, and that awareness has fed her sense that the whole experience is hard to believe, but for her the triggers do not feel symbolic. They feel like openings through which the stalking breaks back into the present.

Over time, this has changed how she lives. In a profession that depends on rapid judgment under pressure, she has become more brittle on days when the office is especially loud, sometimes needing to step into a stairwell to steady herself after a sudden noise sends her heart racing. At home she is more likely to decline social plans if they involve crowded restaurants or drinking. Her partner has tried to reassure her, but Linh has come to dread the look of concern on his face, as though even that confirms how much the stalking still governs her.

By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the sense that her life was being organized around avoiding reminders of something that still did not feel fully real and yet could seize her body as if it were happening now. What frightened her most was not only the memories themselves but the possibility that she would never again be able to move through ordinary places—a loud office, a sidewalk outside a bar, a weekend street full of families—without feeling hijacked by terror. What she hoped for, tentatively, was not to erase what happened but to have it become unmistakably past.
